THOUGHT: This 50-year-old male presents with a painless, firm, mobile, 2.5-cm subcutaneous nodule on the nape of the neck, progressively enlarging over 2 months. Key features include absence of inflammation (no pain, fever, discharge), normal inflammatory markers (normal WBC), and ultrasound showing a well-circumscribed, cystic lesion in the subcutaneous tissue. The skin over the nodule cannot be pinched — this is a classic clinical sign of *infiltration or fixation of the lesion to deeper structures*, but importantly, the lesion is described as *mobile*, which argues against deep invasion or malignancy-related fixation. The cystic, well-circumscribed appearance on ultrasound strongly favors a benign soft-tissue cyst. Among common subcutaneous cysts, an **epidermoid cyst** (formerly called sebaceous cyst, though misnomer) is the most frequent — typically slow-growing, painless, mobile, and located in areas rich in pilosebaceous units (e.g., scalp, neck, back). The nape of the neck is a common site. While lipomas are also common, they are usually more compressible, lobulated, and *solid* (not cystic) on ultrasound — here, imaging specifically describes a *cystic nature*. A pilonidal cyst is unlikely given location (nape, not natal cleft) and lack of sinus tracts or prior drainage. Although the patient has a history of colon cancer (stage not specified), metastatic lymphadenopathy would typically present as a *solid*, often matted or fixed node, possibly with other systemic signs or abnormal LFTs/CBC — none are present; moreover, isolated solitary posterior cervical (nuchal) nodal metastasis from colon cancer is exceedingly rare (colon cancer typically metastasizes to pericolonic, then para-aortic, supraclavicular nodes — not nuchal). Additionally, the ultrasound shows a *subcutaneous* (not nodal) lesion, and there is no associated lymphadenopathy. Other considerations like abscess are ruled out by lack of inflammation, normal WBC, and chronicity (2 months without change in character). Dermatofibroma is typically smaller (<1 cm), firm, tethered to skin (‘dimple sign’), and solid. Sebaceous cysts/epidermoid cysts classically present as slow-growing, asymptomatic, mobile, subcutaneous, cystic nodules — matching all clinical and imaging features.

DIAGNOSIS: Epidermoid cyst
